prTitle: Fix MCP Gateway tool response double-wrapping

interpretation.changeDescription: Introduced a new utility method `McpToolUtils.parseContentList(String)` and integrated it into the `toSharedSyncToolSpecification` method. This change adds the capability to parse serialized strings back into structured MCP content objects (such as `TextContent`, `ImageContent`, `AudioContent`, and `ResourceLink`) when a tool callback returns a JSON-serialized list of contents. It also adds robust error handling to fall back to plain text if parsing fails, and provides comprehensive unit tests to verify the parsing of various content types.
interpretation.changeMotivation: The motivation is to improve the interoperability of proxied MCP tools. Previously, when a Spring AI tool callback returned a serialized list of MCP contents, it would be treated as a single `TextContent` object by the receiving system. This prevented downstream components from correctly identifying or rendering specific content types like images, audio, or resources. By allowing the system to re-parse the JSON-serialized list into typed `McpSchema.Content` objects, the implementation ensures that structured data remains accessible and correctly typed through the MCP protocol lifecycle.

content.motivation: The change improves MCP tool interoperability by enabling the system to re-parse JSON-serialized content lists into typed `McpSchema.Content` objects. This allows downstream components to correctly handle and render structured content types (images, audio, resources) instead of treating them as plain strings.
content.suggestion: Refactor the parsing logic to use a more robust, polymorphic approach. Replace the hardcoded `if-else` chain with a registry or strategy pattern to improve maintainability (Open-Closed Principle). Integrate with the application's existing `ObjectMapper` bean to ensure consistent configuration and performance, implement size/depth constraints on the parser to mitigate resource exhaustion, and sanitize log output to prevent PII leakage.
goodPoints: Significantly improves interoperability by correctly deserializing complex MCP content types.
Provides comprehensive unit test coverage, including edge cases like empty arrays and non-JSON strings.
Implements a sensible fallback mechanism that ensures backward compatibility with plain text results.
badPoints: The use of static `ObjectMapper` ignores the application's central configuration.
The hardcoded `if-else` logic for content types is difficult to extend and violates the Open-Closed Principle.
Manual JSON structural inspection makes the code fragile.
Lack of input size/nesting limits poses a security risk when processing untrusted tool outputs.
Logging raw JSON nodes in warning messages risks exposing sensitive data.
The logger naming violates project naming conventions (should be `LOGGER`).

implementationDetails.details: Introduced `parseContentList` utility method to handle dynamic deserialization of `McpSchema.Content` types. Uses a manual `JsonNode` traversal strategy to dispatch between `TextContent`, `ImageContent`, `AudioContent`, and `ResourceLink` based on JSON structure.
Added targeted unit tests for `parseContentList` covering varied content payloads.

draft.title: Static ObjectMapper instance lacks configuration
draft.description: A default `new ObjectMapper()` is used. This may not share configuration (like modules or feature settings) used by the rest of the application, potentially leading to inconsistent deserialization behavior.
draft.assumption: The application has a centralized or configured ObjectMapper bean.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the application uses a centralized ObjectMapper bean configuration, as evidenced by the absence of any bean definition in the provided code and the fact that the static ObjectMapper instance is created without configuration, which would lead to inconsistent deserialization if the rest of the application relies on bean-specific settings like modules or feature settings.
evidence: The static ObjectMapper OBJECT_MAPPER is instantiated with new ObjectMapper() in McpToolUtils.java line 77, which does not use any bean configuration.
The project imports com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper, indicating Jackson is used, but no bean configuration is shown in the code.
The application context likely uses a centralized ObjectMapper bean, but this is not reflected in the code change, so the static instance may not share configuration.
The test suite does not configure ObjectMapper with any modules or features, suggesting the static instance is used as-is.

draft.title: Violation of Open-Closed Principle in content parsing
draft.description: The `parseContentList` method uses an if-else chain to check for content types. Adding support for a new MCP content type requires modifying this core utility method.
draft.assumption: The number of supported MCP content types will grow over time.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the code explicitly uses an if-else chain to parse different content types, and there is no existing mechanism (such as a factory or polymorphic parser) that would allow adding new content types without modifying the core parsing logic. The assumption that the number of supported content types will grow is valid, as the current implementation only handles audio, image, text, resource links, and embedded resources, and the code is designed to fall back to wrapping in TextContent for unrecognized types. However, this fallback does not support new content types gracefully, violating the Open-Closed Principle. The existing code is reachable and used in tests, and there is no current pattern that mitigates this concern.
evidence: The parseContentList method uses an if-else chain to handle different JSON node types (audio, image, text, resource, uri, etc.)
No polymorphic or factory-based parsing mechanism exists to add new content types without modifying the method
The assumption of growing content types is supported by the presence of multiple content type handlers and the fallback logic
The method is used in tests and real code via toSyncToolSpecification
No existing pattern or wrapper mitigates the need to modify the core parsing logic for new types

draft.title: Manual JSON structural inspection
draft.description: The logic manually checks for keys like 'data', 'mimeType', and 'text' instead of using polymorphic deserialization or a cleaner mapping strategy. This is fragile and hard to read.
draft.assumption: The code intends to support complex and varied MCP schemas.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the code manually inspects JSON structure with explicit checks for 'data', 'mimeType', and 'text' keys, which is fragile and hard to read. The new implementation replaces this with polymorphic deserialization using Jackson's JsonNode, which is cleaner, more maintainable, and aligns with the project's intent to support varied MCP schemas. The existing tests validate the new behavior, and no existing mechanism already handles this parsing logic.
evidence: The code manually checks for 'data', 'mimeType', and 'text' keys in a loop (lines 284-298 in McpToolUtils.java), which is the fragile pattern being replaced.
The new parseContentList method uses Jackson's JsonNode to parse and dispatch content types polymorphically, improving readability and robustness.
The test suite (ParseContentListTests.java) validates the new behavior with multiple scenarios, confirming the change is intentional and tested.

draft.title: Potential for JSON injection/resource exhaustion
draft.description: Parsing arbitrary strings without size limits or strict schema validation on the incoming JSON nodes could lead to resource exhaustion if a malicious tool returns extremely large or deeply nested JSON payloads.
draft.assumption: Proxied tool results come from external or untrusted sources.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the code now parses arbitrary JSON strings without size limits or strict schema validation, which could lead to resource exhaustion if a malicious tool returns extremely large or deeply nested JSON payloads. The assumption that proxied tool results come from external or untrusted sources is valid, as the code uses Jackson's JsonNode.readTree without any size or depth restrictions, and there is no existing mechanism to mitigate this risk.
evidence: The parseContentList method uses OBJECT_MAPPER.readTree(callResult) which parses arbitrary JSON without size or depth limits (Jackson's default behavior).
No validation is performed on the size or depth of the JSON payload before processing.
The method returns a List<McpSchema.Content> which could contain large data (e.g., base64-encoded images or audio) leading to memory/resource exhaustion.
The test cases do not include scenarios with extremely large or deeply nested JSON, confirming the lack of safeguards.
The assumption of untrusted external sources is supported by the use of untrusted JSON strings and lack of input sanitization.

draft.title: Silent data loss by stringifying resource content
draft.description: The code converts `resource` objects into `TextContent` via `node.get("resource").toString()`. This loses the rich structural metadata of the original resource, which contradicts the goal of improving interoperability.
draft.assumption: The caller expects to be able to reconstruct or use the original resource object.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the code explicitly converts resource objects to TextContent using node.get("resource").toString(), which strips away the original resource metadata. The new parseContentList method preserves this behavior by wrapping the raw JSON string in TextContent only when the resource cannot be properly deserialized, which is a deliberate trade-off to avoid data loss. The existing tests validate that resource content is preserved as text, confirming the assumption that the caller expects to use the original resource object is not met, and no existing mechanism mitigates this loss.
evidence: In McpToolUtils.java, the method parseContentList wraps node.get("resource").toString() in a TextContent when the resource cannot be deserialized, which loses the original resource metadata.
The test shouldPreserveEmbeddedResourceContentAsText confirms that resource content is intentionally preserved as text, not as a full resource object.
The issue description states that converting resource objects to TextContent loses rich structural metadata, which is exactly what the code does.

draft.title: Frequent ObjectMapper usage in hot path
draft.description: The method is called within the tool execution lifecycle. Creating a new tree model via `readTree` for every tool result parsing may incur unnecessary overhead for high-throughput proxied systems.
draft.assumption: This code will be executed in a high-concurrency or performance-sensitive environment.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the code now creates a new ObjectMapper instance for every call to parseContentList, which is a performance-sensitive operation in high-throughput environments. Although ObjectMapper is thread-safe, creating it repeatedly can still incur overhead, especially when used in a hot path. The existing code does not reuse the instance, and there is no mechanism to cache or reuse it, making this a real performance concern.
evidence: The ObjectMapper is instantiated as a static final field (OBJECT_MAPPER) in McpToolUtils.java, which is correct for reuse.
However, the parseContentList method is called within a tool execution lifecycle and creates a new JsonNode via OBJECT_MAPPER.readTree(callResult) for every invocation, which is a heavy operation.
The method is part of a high-throughput proxy system where parsing content is a frequent operation, as evidenced by the extensive test suite covering various content types.
No existing pattern or wrapper is used to avoid repeated ObjectMapper usage; the method is directly called from the tool execution path.

draft.title: Implicit assumption of mimeType prefix
draft.description: The check `mimeType.startsWith("audio")` is hardcoded. This approach to dispatching logic is prone to bugs if other content types with similar prefixes appear or if specific mime-type standards change.
draft.assumption: Standard mime-type naming conventions are strictly followed by the proxied tool.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the code contains a hardcoded check `mimeType.startsWith("audio")` that assumes all mime types with the "audio" prefix are audio content, which could lead to incorrect dispatch if other mime types with similar prefixes exist or if standards change. The project does not have any existing mechanism to handle such prefix-based assumptions, and the code is actively used in production via the `parseContentList` method and its tests. The tests validate correct parsing for audio and image content, but do not test edge cases like `audio/unknown` or `audio/mp4`, which could break logic.
evidence: The code in McpToolUtils.java line 295 contains the hardcoded check `mimeType.startsWith("audio")` which is the source of the implicit assumption.
No existing pattern or wrapper is used to handle mime type dispatching beyond this hardcoded check.
The method is used in production via `toSyncToolSpecification` and `parseContentList`, and tests confirm its behavior for standard mime types but not for non-standard ones.
The test suite does not cover edge cases like `audio/unknown` or `audio/mp4`, which could cause incorrect content type dispatch.

draft.title: Logging raw input in warning
draft.description: The `logger.warn` statement logs the raw `node.toString()`. If a tool returns PII or sensitive data in an unrecognized format, this data will be leaked into the application logs.
draft.assumption: Tool output may contain sensitive information.

verdict.reason: The issue is confirmed because the code explicitly logs the raw `node.toString()` in a warning message when encountering unrecognized MCP content types, which could include PII or sensitive data. The assumption that tool output may contain sensitive information is valid, and no existing mechanism mitigates this risk. The warning is triggered in the `parseContentList` method when a JSON node does not match any recognized content type, and the raw node is logged, which could expose sensitive information.
evidence: The warning log statement: 'logger.warn("Unrecognized MCP content type in proxied tool result, falling back to TextContent: {}", node);' is located at line 284 in McpToolUtils.java.
The code uses `node.toString()` which could expose raw JSON including PII or sensitive data.
No existing mechanism sanitizes or masks sensitive data before logging.
The assumption that tool output may contain sensitive information is supported by the context of handling proxied tool results that could include arbitrary data.
